title: Weather and seasons
goal: Talk about the weather — the number one conversation starter in Denmark — and name the seasons, temperatures and clothes.
bekal: use *det er* and *det bliver* for the weather now and later
name the four seasons and what happens in each
use the present tense to talk about the future
wave: Review **unit 10** first: take five of your own sentences, move the time expression to the front, and make sure the subject jumps behind the verb.

dialogs.title: Dialogue — Typisk dansk vejr
dialogs.intro: Early November. Budi and Mette are standing under the bus shelter, waiting for the rain to stop.

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.text: Sikke et vejr! Det har regnet hele dagen.
lines.id: What weather! It's been raining all day.
lines.literal: what a weather! it has rained whole day-the.

lines.speaker: Mette:
lines.text: Velkommen til november. Sådan er det hver dag nu.
lines.id: Welcome to November. It's like this every day now.
lines.literal: welcome to November. so is it every day now.

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.text: Bliver det bedre i næste uge?
lines.id: Will it get better next week?
lines.literal: becomes it better in next week?

lines.speaker: Mette:
lines.text: Nej. Det bliver koldere. Og mørkere.
lines.id: No. It'll get colder. And darker.
lines.literal: no. it becomes colder. and darker.

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.text: Hvor koldt bliver det om vinteren?
lines.id: How cold does it get in winter?
lines.literal: how cold becomes it in winter-the?

lines.speaker: Mette:
lines.text: Omkring nul grader. Nogle gange minus fem.
lines.id: Around zero degrees. Sometimes minus five.
lines.literal: around zero degrees. some times minus five.

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.text: Minus fem! I Jakarta er det tredive grader hele året.
lines.id: Minus five! In Jakarta it's thirty degrees all year round.
lines.literal: minus five! in Jakarta is it thirty degrees whole year-the.

lines.speaker: Mette:
lines.text: Så bliver det en interessant vinter for dig.
lines.id: Then it'll be an interesting winter for you.
lines.literal: then becomes it an interesting winter for you.

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.text: Hvad gør man, når det er så mørkt?
lines.id: What do people do when it's that dark?
lines.literal: what does one, when it is so dark?

lines.speaker: Mette:
lines.text: Man tænder lys, laver varm mad og hygger sig. Det er derfor hygge findes.
lines.id: You light candles, cook warm food and get cozy. That's why hygge exists.
lines.literal: one lights candles, makes warm food and cozies oneself. it is therefore hygge is-found.

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.text: Nu forstår jeg endelig det ord.
lines.id: Now I finally understand that word.
lines.literal: now understand I finally that word.

notes: **Det er** is for the present state, **det bliver** for what is coming or changing. *At blive* = to become, and it's one of the most important verbs in Danish. It also means "to stay": *jeg bliver hjemme* = I'm staying at home.

**Present tense for the future.** Notice there isn't a single future auxiliary in this dialog. *Bliver det bedre i næste uge?* uses the present tense for next week — like English "I'm leaving tomorrow", but Danish does it far more often, where English would usually need *will*.
**Koldere, mørkere** — the ending **-ere** compares, like English *-er*. *kold → koldere → koldest*.
**Sådan** = "like that, so". A very handy little word: *Sådan er det.* (That's how it is.) Also used as a satisfied exclamation when something works: *Sådan!*
**Grader.** Denmark uses Celsius, and temperatures below zero are *minus*: *minus fem grader*, or more casually *fem graders frost*.
**At tænde lys.** Denmark burns more candles per person than any other country, and that is directly linked to its long nights. In December the sun rises at 8:30 and sets at 3:30.
**At hygge sig** — the reflexive verb from unit 9, used exactly like that: *vi hygger os* = we're having a cozy time together.
**Endelig** = finally. Don't confuse it with *til sidst* (in the end, as the last step). *Endelig* carries a sense of relief.

grammars.title: Det er and det bliver
body: Weather and general conditions always use *det* as a dummy subject — exactly like *it* in English (*it is raining*). Good news: this works just the way you're used to.
after: Notice that weather adjectives always end in **-t**: *koldt*, *varmt*, *mørkt*, *dejligt* — because they describe *det*, and *det* is an et-word. It's the same pattern you saw in unit 3.
⚠️ *At regne* has two completely different meanings: "to rain" and "to calculate". Context tells them apart, and misunderstandings almost never happen.

grammars.title: The future without an extra verb
body: Danish has no separate future tense. There are three ways to talk about the future, and the most common one is also the simplest.
after: When in doubt, use the first row. *Jeg kommer i morgen* is perfectly correct and sounds the most natural.
⚠️ Danish *vil* mainly means **want**, not a future marker like English *will*. *Jeg vil spise* means "I want to eat", not "I will eat". This is one of the biggest traps for English speakers.

blocks.text: *Dejligt* is the most Danish all-purpose word of praise: *dejligt vejr*, *dejlig mad*, *en dejlig dag*. If you could learn only one positive adjective, learn this one.

blocks.title: Why weather matters so much in Danish conversation
items: Weather is a safe, neutral conversation starter in a country that's uncomfortable with personal small talk. Asking a stranger "where do you live?" feels too forward; commenting on the rain does not.
Ready-made lines: *Sikke et vejr!*, *Dejligt vejr i dag, ikke?*, *Det bliver vist bedre i morgen.*
There's a Danish saying you'll hear again and again: *Der findes ikke dårligt vejr, kun forkert påklædning* — "There's no such thing as bad weather, only the wrong clothes."

blocks.text: Notice how they're used with **om**: *om foråret*, *om sommeren*, *om efteråret*, *om vinteren* — all with the definite ending. Same pattern as the parts of the day in unit 8: *om morgenen*, *om aftenen*.

The difference in daylight in Denmark is extreme and really shapes daily life: in **June** the sun sets around 10:00 p.m. and the sky never gets fully dark; in **December** it sets at 3:30 p.m. For newcomers from places near the equator — where day and night are almost equal all year — this is a bigger adjustment than the temperature.
*Handsker*, *støvler* and *sko* are almost always used in the plural, since they come in pairs. To count them: *et par handsker* (a pair of gloves).
